title: Sacrifice to the Guru
hookLine: satgur vittahu vaariaa: a sacrifice to the Guru, meeting whom I remember the Master (Asa di Var, ang 470)

lines: A SENTENCE, A BOOK, A STRANGER.
THE SAME STREET, THE SAME JOB.
cards: A single sentence that rearranged everything. A book picked up by accident. A stranger on a train.
Some lives turn on one afternoon like that. Ask what changed, though, and it's rarely the world. The street was the same street, the job the same job.
What changed was the seeing. On day five hundred thirty-eight, Guru Nanak said he'd give himself a hundred times a day to the Guru who made angels out of men.
Today's pauri comes back to that gratitude, and says exactly what changed.

teach.b: The pauri is on ang 470, the same page as the tree and the scale. It opens: satgur vittahu vaariaa. I am a sacrifice to the True Guru.

Vaariaa is a word of love and offering, the feeling behind the custom of circling something precious around a loved one's head and giving it away. Then, in paraphrase: meeting the Guru, I remembered the Master.

teach.h: GIAN ANJAN: WISDOM ON THE EYES.
teach.b: The Guru gave the ointment of wisdom, and with these same eyes I now see the world as it is. Gian anjan. Anjan is the dark ointment people put along the eyes.
The eyes don't change. What they can see does. That's the turning point.
Before, the world was koorh, the false king and the tall tree, all looking solid and impressive.

teach.h: THE SAME EYES, A NEW WORLD.
teach.b: After, the same world is seen clearly, with the One in it. Then the pauri warns about the other road. Traders who leave the Master and attach to another, it says, are drowned.
And it ends with a picture: the True Guru is the boat, though few realize it, and by grace the Guru carries people across.
In Sikh teaching, the Guru is the One's word reaching a person: through the human Gurus, and now through the Guru Granth Sahib.

In this pauri, the sacrifice is gratitude: offering yourself to whatever opened your eyes, and keeping them open. This week's saloks were all about seeing: ego, books, koorh, truth, pain, sweetness, the tree.
Here's what lets you see them.

how: Sikhs hear this pauri in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and express gratitude to the Guru daily in Ardas and in bowing before the Guru Granth Sahib.

o: a prayer for a safe journey
a vow to fight for the Guru
an offering of yourself, in love

games.q: the pauri of gratitude — tap the pairs.
p: the ointment of wisdom on the eyes

s: the Guru's ointment gives a person new eyes
the same eyes now see the world as it is.
the pauri calls the True Guru a boat
few realize it, and by grace the Guru carries people across.
in this pauri, the sacrifice is a dramatic act of giving up one's life
here it is gratitude: offering yourself to what opened your eyes.

games.q: you've met the Guru and your eyes have been opened. what does the pauri say you now see?
o: a different world, far from this one.
this same world, seen as it really is.
nothing; the eyes close in meditation.
games.why: the Guru gave the ointment of wisdom, and with these eyes the world is seen. the eyes don't change; what they see does.

practice: Let one moment come back when your way of seeing changed: a person, a line, a day. Picture the before and the after, and notice what you see now that you couldn't see then; if gratitude comes, let it come.
If you pray, say Waheguru softly, as a thank-you.

wordCard.voice: Vaariaa, a sacrifice or offering: satgur vittahu vaariaa, I offer myself to the True Guru, who put wisdom on my eyes, so I see the same world truly.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: I am a sacrifice to the True Guru; the opening of the pauri.

carryVoice: Your line: the turning point. The eyes stay the same; the seeing changes. See you tomorrow.
